content_metadata.description: This video presents the development and application of Implicit Displacement Fields for improved 3D shape representation, addressing the limitations of existing methods and introducing novel solutions.

qAndA.answer: Their ability to represent high-frequency geometry details is limited by the spectral bias of neural networks.
qAndA.question: What is the main limitation of existing neural implicit functions when representing 3D shapes?

qAndA.answer: Spatial partitioning and increasing the signal's frequency.
qAndA.question: What are the two main directions explored in related work to address this limitation?

qAndA.answer: It introduces constraints by making the high-frequency signal dependent on the low-frequency base, ensuring more stable optimization.
qAndA.question: How does the proposed Implicit Displacement Field solution address the limitations of the naive approach?

qAndA.answer: It avoids the discrete nature of classic methods and allows for a more accurate and robust representation of details.
qAndA.question: What are the advantages of generalizing classic displacement maps to the continuous R3 domain?

qAndA.answer: It enables the transfer of learned details to unseen target shapes without requiring parameterization or correspondence mapping, opening up possibilities for shape manipulation and modeling.
qAndA.question: How does the concept of transferability enhance the applicability of Implicit Displacement Fields?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: We present implicit displacement fields, novel neuro-implicit representation for detailed
3D geometries.
Neuro-implicit functions have theoretically infinite resolution, but in practice, a variability
to represent high-friculty geometry details is limited by neural network spectral bias.
This work aims to reformulate the existing neuro-implicit shift representation for more robust,
efficient and accurate geometry-detail reconstruction.
One direction the TACOVS issue focuses on spatial partition, but doing so makes the geometry
resolution dependent on the spatial resolution, incurring cubic memory growth.
The other direction focuses on increasing a signal's frequency, but high-friculty signals
are extremely difficult to optimize, often falling to overfitting low-communima and even
divergence.
Our idea is to decompose a surface into a smooth base and a high-friculty displacement.
In particular, we make this separation happen automatically by utilizing periodic activation
functions and setting the frequency parameters for the base and displacement respectively
lower and higher.
So this is not all.
Now you can add in a low and high-friculty parts together leads to a very bad result,
as the high-frequency component causes optimization problems in lack of constraints.
Our solution is inspired by a classic shape deformation technique, displacement mapping,
which creates detailed surface from a smooth one by displacing sample points along the
normal directions.
Obviously though, this definition is discrete and is defined only on the surface.
Hence our work proposes a theoretically grounded extension to generalize classic displacement
maps to the continuous R3 domain.
We pay extra attention in a formulation to avoid requiring ground truth SDF values for
supervision, such that we can directly learn from the point cloud by solving an economic
equation and boundary constraints.
Combining this idea with a few other architectural and training optimizations that we introduce
in our paper, our model outperforms the state of the art method in detailed representation
while having only a fraction of parameters.
Furthermore, we also explore the transferability of the implicit displacement field by untying
the displacement prediction from the global coordinates with a carefully constructed
transferable feature.
One application of this is detailed transfer.
For example, given the detailed source shape on the left, we learn a transferable displacement
field to capture its surface details.
Once trained, this detail can be transferred to a new unseen target by simply swapping the
base shapes. No parameterization nor corresponding mapping is required.
Compared to existing detailed transfer with explicit representation,
implicit shape editing bypasses common artifacts such as self-intersections.
In summary, we propose implicit displacement fields, which extend explicit discrete
displacement mapping to implicit formulation. In doing so, we achieve frequency-based
geometry decomposition in an unsupervised manner.
Lastly, we introduce transferability to implicit displacement fields, thus opening new
opportunities for implicit geometry manipulation and shape modeling.
Thank you for your attention.
